summary: Specifies how to use the DES encryption algorithm in cipher feedback mode with the Telnet encryption option. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This picks the older DES scrambler for hiding Telnet text.

subtitle: DES encryption in cipher feedback mode for Telnet.

tldr.problem: Telnet sessions transmit commands and responses in plain text, vulnerable to eavesdropping. The Telnet encryption option allows negotiating encryption, and DES in cipher feedback mode is one cipher choice.
tldr.mechanism: Telnet peers exchange an 8-byte initial vector, negotiate a shared encryption key, and then encrypt data using DES applied in 64-bit cipher feedback mode. The cipher turns the shared key into a keystream that is XORed with the plaintext.
tldr.outcome: This provides confidentiality for Telnet traffic, though cipher feedback mode does not guarantee integrity and offers only limited protection against active attacks.

today: RFC 2952 is an Informational RFC published in September 2000. It documents encryption option support for Telnet at a time when Telnet was still widely used. DES is now considered cryptographically weak; modern systems use stronger algorithms and prefer SSH over Telnet.

sections.title: Telnet Encryption and DES
sections.content: This RFC specifies how to use the DES (Data Encryption Standard) algorithm in cipher feedback mode as an encryption mechanism for the Telnet protocol. DES CFB64 is one of several cipher options for the Telnet ENCRYPTION option. The method operates on 64-bit blocks of data, encrypting Telnet traffic to prevent passive eavesdropping on commands and responses sent over the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet sends commands and responses over the network, and anyone listening can see them. This method scrambles the data using DES so only the intended recipient can read it.

sections.title: The Negotiation and Encryption Process
sections.content: The two sides of the connection exchange an 8-byte initial vector in clear text. One side (WILL ENCRYPT) generates a random initial vector and sends it via the CFB64_IV command; the other side (DO ENCRYPT) responds with CFB64_IV_OK or CFB64_IV_BAD. After accepting the vector and negotiating a shared key, they can exchange encrypted data. The cipher applies DES to successive blocks, XORing the result with plaintext data to produce ciphertext, using the previous ciphertext as input to the next DES operation.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides start by agreeing on a secret number (a key) and a random starting point (the initial vector). Then they use DES to scramble each 64-bit chunk of data, feeding the scrambled output back into the next chunk.

sections.title: Security Properties and Limitations
sections.content: Cipher feedback mode provides encryption but not authentication or integrity checking. An active attacker who can predict the plaintext has a limited ability to modify it by changing ciphertext blocks, though the attack is constrained to modifying 8-byte chunks and corrupting the following block, making detection likely. The trade-off is that adding a message authentication code would increase overhead significantly on slow links. DES keys must be at least 8 bytes; longer keys have parity bits corrected to match DES requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The method hides what you are typing, but it does not promise that someone did not tamper with the message on the way. An attacker might be able to change small parts if they know what you are sending, but it is pretty obvious when they do.
